title: I. Father Zossima And His Visitors
paragraphs: Alyosha entered his elder’s cell with an anxious, aching heart, and he stopped in the doorway, almost astonished. He had been afraid of finding a sick man at his last gasp, perhaps unconscious. Instead the elder was sitting up in his chair. He was weak and worn out, yet his face was bright and cheerful. Visitors were gathered around him, and they were talking together quietly and happily. In fact he had left his bed only a quarter of an hour before Alyosha came. The visitors had assembled in his cell earlier and sat waiting for him to wake. Father Païssy had assured them with great confidence that “the teacher would get up and, as he had promised that morning, talk once more with those dear to his heart.” Father Païssy trusted this promise completely, as he trusted every word the dying elder spoke. Suppose he had found him unconscious, or even seen him breathe his last, and still held his promise that he would rise and say good-bye. Perhaps even then he would not have believed in death. He would have gone on expecting the dead man to revive and keep his word. That morning, as he lay down to sleep, Father Zossima had told him flatly: “I shall not die without the joy of one more conversation with you, beloved of my heart. I shall look once more on your dear face and pour out my heart to you again.” The monks who had gathered for this probably last talk with Father Zossima had been his devoted friends for many years. There were four of them. The first two were Father Iosif and Father Païssy. The third was Father Mihaïl, warden of the hermitage, a man not very old and far from learned. He came of humble people, and he had a strong will and a steadfast faith. He looked austere, but he was deeply tender, though he clearly kept this hidden, as if almost ashamed of it. The fourth, Father Anfim, was a very old, humble little monk from the poorest peasant class. He was nearly illiterate and very quiet, and he hardly spoke to anyone. He was the humblest of the humble, and he looked as if something vast and terrible, beyond his understanding, had frightened him. Father Zossima was deeply fond of this timid man and always treated him with marked respect. Yet perhaps he had said less to him than to anyone he had ever known, although he had spent years wandering with him over holy Russia. That was long ago, forty years back, when Father Zossima was just beginning his monastic life in a poor little monastery at Kostroma. Soon afterward he had gone with Father Anfim on a journey to collect alms for that poor monastery.

They were all in the bedroom, which, as we said before, was very small. There was hardly room for the four of them to sit round Father Zossima on chairs brought in from the sitting room (Porfiry the novice stood). Darkness was already coming on. The room was lit by lamps and by the candles in front of the ikons.
Seeing Alyosha standing embarrassed in the doorway, Father Zossima smiled at him joyfully and held out his hand.
“Welcome, my quiet one. Welcome, my dear, you are here too. I knew you would come.”
Alyosha went to him and bowed to the ground before him, and he wept. Something rose up from deep in his heart. His soul was shaking, and he wanted to sob aloud.

“Come now, do not weep over me yet,” said Father Zossima with a smile, laying his right hand on Alyosha’s head. “You see, I am sitting up and talking. Maybe I shall live another twenty years, as that good dear woman from Vishegorye wished me yesterday, with her little Lizaveta in her arms. God bless the mother and the little girl Lizaveta.” He crossed himself. “Porfiry, did you take her offering where I told you?”

He meant the sixty copecks that the cheerful woman had brought him the day before, to be passed on “to someone poorer than me.” Gifts like this are always made from money earned by one’s own labor, and they are offered as a penance freely chosen. The previous evening the elder had sent Porfiry to a widow whose house had recently burned down, and who had been going about begging with her children since the fire. Porfiry quickly replied that he had handed over the money as instructed, “from an unknown benefactress.”

“Get up, my dear boy,” the elder went on, speaking to Alyosha. “I want to look at you. Have you been home? Did you see your brother?” Alyosha thought it strange that he asked so confidently and so exactly about just one of his brothers. But which one? Perhaps he had sent Alyosha out yesterday and again today for that brother’s sake.
“I have seen one of my brothers,” answered Alyosha.
“I mean the elder one, the one I bowed down to.”
“I only saw him yesterday. I could not find him today,” said Alyosha.

“Hurry and find him. Go again tomorrow, and hurry. Drop everything and hurry. You may still be in time to prevent something terrible. Yesterday I bowed down before the great suffering that awaits him.”

He fell silent all at once and seemed lost in thought. His words were strange. Father Iosif, who had seen the scene the day before, exchanged a look with Father Païssy. Alyosha could not keep himself from asking:
“Father and teacher,” he began, deeply moved, “your words are too obscure.... What is this suffering that awaits him?”

“Do not ask. Yesterday I seemed to see something terrible ... as if his whole future were written in his eyes. There came a look into his eyes—and I was struck with horror at once, at what that man is preparing for himself. Once or twice in my life I have seen that look on a man’s face ... showing, as it were, the fate in store for him, and that fate, alas, came to pass. I sent you to him, Alexey, because I thought your brotherly face would help him. But everything, and all our fates, come from the Lord. ‘Except a corn of wheat fall into the ground and die, it abideth alone; but if it die, it bringeth forth much fruit.’ Remember that. As for you, Alexey, many times I have blessed you silently because of your face. Know that,” added the elder, with a gentle smile. “This is what I think of you. You will leave these walls, but you will live in the world like a monk. You will have many enemies, yet even your enemies will love you. Life will bring you many misfortunes, but in them you will find your happiness, and you will bless life and make others bless it, which is what matters most. Well, that is your character. Fathers and teachers,” he said to his friends with a tender smile, “until today I have never told even him why this young man’s face is so dear to me. Now I will tell you. His face has been for me a remembrance and a prophecy together. When I was a child, at the dawn of my life, I had an elder brother who died before my eyes at the age of seventeen. As my life went on, I gradually came to believe that this brother was meant as a guide and a sign from above for me. Had he not entered my life, I should never have become a monk and set foot on this precious path, or so I think. He appeared to me first in my childhood, and now, at the end of my pilgrimage, it seems he has come to me a second time. It is marvelous, fathers and teachers. Alexey bears some resemblance to him in face, though not a great one. But in spirit he seems to me so like him that many times I have taken him for that young man, my brother, come back to me mysteriously at the end of my journey to remind and inspire me. I was truly amazed at so strange a fancy in myself. Do you hear this, Porfiry?” He turned to the novice who attended him. “Many times I have seen a look of mortification in your face, because I love Alexey more than you. Now you know the reason. But I love you too, know that, and many times I was grieved by your mortification. Dear friends, I want to tell you about that youth, my brother, for no one who has been in my life was more precious, more full of meaning, or more touching. My heart is full of tenderness, and at this moment I look at my whole life as though I were living it over again.”

Here I must point out that this last conversation of Father Zossima with the friends who visited him on the last day of his life has been partly preserved in writing. Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov put it down from memory, some time after his elder’s death. Whether it was only the talk of that evening, or whether he also wove in notes from earlier conversations with his teacher, I cannot say. In his account Father Zossima speaks on without a break, as if he were telling his life to his friends as a story. Yet other accounts leave no doubt that the talk that evening was shared by all. The guests did not interrupt Father Zossima often, but they did talk, and perhaps they even told some stories of their own. Besides, Father Zossima could not have gone on without pause. He sometimes gasped for breath and lost his voice, and he even lay down on his bed to rest, though he did not sleep, and his visitors stayed in their seats. Once or twice Father Païssy broke in to read from the Gospel. It is also worth noting that not one of them thought he would die that night. In the evening, after his deep sleep during the day, he seemed to have suddenly found fresh strength, and it carried him through this long conversation. It was like a last effort of love, and it gave him marvelous energy. It lasted only a short time, however, for his life was cut short at once.... But of that later. For now I will add only that I have chosen to keep to the account written by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov. It will be shorter and less wearying, though, as I must say again, Alyosha took much from earlier conversations and added it here.
Notes on the Life of the late Priest and Monk, the Elder Zossima, taken down from his own words by Alexey Fyodorovitch Karamazov.
BIOGRAPHICAL NOTES
_(a)_ _Father Zossima’s Brother_

Beloved fathers and teachers, I was born in a remote northern province, in the town of V. My father was a gentleman by birth, but he had no great standing or rank. He died when I was two years old, and I have no memory of him at all. He left my mother a small house built of wood and a modest fortune, but enough to keep her and her children comfortably. There were two of us, my elder brother Markel and I. He was eight years older than I was. He had a hasty, irritable temper, but he was kind-hearted and never ironic. He was remarkably silent, especially at home, with me, with his mother and with the servants. He did well at school but could not get along with his schoolmates, though he never quarreled with them, or so my mother has told me. Six months before his death, when he was seventeen, he became friends with a political exile. This man had been sent from Moscow to our town for freethinking, and he lived there alone. He was a fine scholar who had distinguished himself in philosophy at the university. Something drew him to Markel, and he often asked him to visit. That winter the young man spent whole evenings with him, until the exile was called to Petersburg to take up his post again, at his own request, since he had powerful friends.

It was the start of Lent, and Markel would not fast. He was rude and laughed at it. “It is all silly nonsense, and there is no God,” he said, to the horror of my mother, the servants, and me as well. Though I was only nine, I was appalled at hearing such words. We had four servants, all serfs. I remember my mother selling one of them, the cook Afimya, a lame elderly woman, for sixty paper roubles, and hiring a free servant in her place.

In the sixth week of Lent my brother fell ill. He had never been strong and was prone to consumption. He was tall but thin and frail-looking, with a very pleasing face. I suppose he had caught cold. In any case, the doctor who came soon whispered to my mother that it was galloping consumption and that he would not live out the spring. My mother began to weep. She was careful not to alarm my brother, but she begged him to go to church, to confess and to receive the sacrament, since he could still get about. This angered him, and he said something profane about the church. Still, he grew thoughtful. He guessed at once that he was gravely ill, and that this was why his mother was pleading with him to confess and take the sacrament. In fact he had known for a long time that he was far from well. A year earlier he had remarked coolly at dinner, to our mother and me, “I will not be long among you. I may not live another year.” Now those words seemed like a prophecy.

Three days went by, and Holy Week arrived. On Tuesday morning my brother began going to church. “I am doing this only for you, mother, to please and comfort you,” he said. My mother wept for joy and for grief. “His end must be near,” she thought, “if he has changed so much.” But he could not go to church for long. He took to his bed, and so he had to confess and receive the sacrament at home.

Easter came late that year, and the days were bright and fine and full of fragrance. I remember that he coughed all night and slept badly, but in the morning he dressed and tried to sit in an armchair. That is how I remember him, sitting there sweet and gentle, smiling, his face bright and joyful in spite of his illness. A marvelous change had come over him, and his spirit seemed transformed. The old nurse would come in and say, “Let me light the lamp before the holy image, my dear.” Earlier he would not have let her, and would have blown it out.
“Light it, light it, dear. I was a wretch to stop you before. You are praying when you light the lamp, and I am praying when I rejoice to see you. So we are praying to the same God.”

We thought those words strange, and mother would go to her room and weep. But when she went in to him she dried her eyes and looked cheerful. “Mother, do not weep, my darling,” he would say. “I have a long life ahead of me, a long time to rejoice with you, and life is glad and joyful.”
“Oh, my dear boy, how can you speak of joy when you lie feverish all night, coughing as if you would tear yourself apart?”
“Do not cry, mother,” he would answer. “Life is paradise, and we are all in paradise, but we refuse to see it. If we wanted to, heaven would be on earth by tomorrow.”

Everyone marveled at what he said, so strange and sure was his way of speaking. We were all moved, and we wept. Friends came to see us. “Dear ones,” he would say to them, “what have I done to deserve your love? How can you love someone like me? And how was it that I never knew, and never valued it before?”

Whenever the servants came in, he would keep saying, “Dear, kind people, why do you do so much for me? Do I deserve to be waited on? If it were God’s will that I should live, I would wait on you, for we should all wait on one another.”
Mother shook her head as she listened. “My darling, it is your illness that makes you talk like this.”

“Mother, darling,” he would say, “there have to be servants and masters. But if so, I will be the servant of my servants, just as they are to me. And there is something else, mother. Each one of us has sinned against all men, and I more than any.”

Mother actually smiled at this, smiled through her tears. “How could you have sinned against all men, and more than all? Robbers and murderers have done that. But what sin have you committed yet, that you hold yourself more guilty than everyone?”

“Mother, little heart of mine,” he said (he had begun to use such strange, tender words then), “little heart of mine, my joy, believe me, each of us is truly responsible to all men, for all men and for everything. I cannot explain it to you, but I feel that it is so, even painfully. And how could we go on living as we did, getting angry and not knowing?”
So he rose each day, more sweet and joyful and loving than the day before. Then the doctor would come, an old German named Eisenschmidt:
“Well, doctor, do I have another day in this world?” he would ask, joking.
“You will have many days yet,” the doctor would answer, “and months and years too.”

“Months and years!” he would cry. “Why reckon in days? One day is enough for a man to know all happiness. My dear ones, why do we quarrel, and try to outdo each other, and nurse grudges? Let us go straight out to the garden and walk and play there, and love and value and kiss one another, and glorify life.”
“Your son cannot last long,” the doctor told my mother, as she went with him to the door. “The illness is reaching his brain.”

The windows of his room opened onto the garden. It was a shady garden with old trees, which were just coming into bud. The first birds of spring were fluttering in the branches and chirping and singing at his windows. As he watched them and admired them, he suddenly began to beg their forgiveness as well: “Birds of heaven, happy birds, forgive me, for I have sinned against you too.” None of us could understand that then, but he wept tears of joy. “Yes,” he said, “God’s glory was all around me, in birds, trees, meadows and sky. Only I lived in shame, dishonoring it all, and I never noticed the beauty and the glory.”
“You are taking too many sins on yourself,” Mother would say, weeping.

“Mother, darling, I am crying for joy, not for grief. I cannot explain it to you, but I like to humble myself before them, because I do not know how to love them enough. If I have sinned against everyone, yet everyone forgives me too, and that is heaven. Am I not in heaven now?”

And he said a great deal more that I do not remember. I do remember going into his room once when nobody else was there. It was a bright evening, the sun was going down, and the whole room was full of light. He beckoned to me and I went over to him. He put his hands on my shoulders and looked into my face, tenderly and lovingly. He said nothing for a minute. He only looked at me like that.
“Well,” he said, “go and play now. Enjoy life for me too.”

So I went out and ran off to play. And many times in my life afterwards I remembered, even with tears, how he told me to enjoy life for him too. He had many other wonderful and beautiful sayings, though we did not understand them at the time. He died in the third week after Easter. He was fully conscious, though he could no longer speak, and he did not change up to his last hour. He looked happy. His eyes shone and searched for us, and he smiled at us and beckoned us. People talked a great deal about his death, even in the town. All this made an impression on me at the time, but not too deep a one, though I cried a good deal at his funeral. I was young then, only a child. Yet a lasting impression, a hidden feeling about it all, stayed in my heart, ready to rise up and answer when its time came. And so indeed it happened.
_(b) Of the Holy Scriptures in the Life of Father Zossima_

I was left alone with my mother. Her friends began to advise her to send me to Petersburg, as other parents did. “You have only one son now,” they said, “and a fair income. If you keep him here, you may be robbing him of a brilliant career.” They suggested that I be sent to Petersburg, to the Cadet Corps, so that I could afterwards enter the Imperial Guard. My mother hesitated for a long time, because it was dreadful to part with her only child. But at last she made up her mind, though not without many tears, believing that she was acting for my happiness. She brought me to Petersburg and placed me in the Cadet Corps, and I never saw her again. For she too died, three years later. She spent those three years mourning and grieving for both of us.

From the house of my childhood I have brought away nothing but precious memories. No memories are more precious than those of early childhood in one’s first home, and that is almost always so, as long as there is any love and harmony in the family at all. Even a bad home can leave precious memories, if only the heart knows how to find what is precious in it. Among my memories of home I count my memories of the Bible, which I was very eager to read as a child. I had a book of Scripture history then, with excellent pictures, called _A Hundred and Four Stories from the Old and New Testament_. I learned to read from it. It lies on my shelf now, and I keep it as a precious relic of the past. But even before I could read, I was moved to devotion for the first time, at eight years old. I remember it well. My mother took me alone to the service on the Monday before Easter. (I do not remember where my brother was.) The day was fine. I remember it today as though I saw it now: the incense rose from the censer and floated softly upwards, and up in the cupola it mingled, in rising waves, with the sunlight streaming through the little window. The sight stirred me, and for the first time in my life I consciously received the seed of God’s word in my heart. A youth came out into the middle of the church carrying a big book. It was so large that I thought he could scarcely carry it. He laid it on the reading desk and opened it and began to read, and suddenly, for the first time, I understood something that was read in the church of God. In the land of Uz there lived a man, righteous and God-fearing, who had great wealth: so many camels, so many sheep and asses. His children feasted, and he loved them dearly and prayed for them. “It may be that my sons have sinned in their feasting.” Then the devil came before the Lord, together with the sons of God, and told the Lord that he had gone up and down the earth and under the earth. “And have you considered my servant Job?” God asked him. God boasted to the devil of His great and holy servant, and the devil laughed at God’s words. “Give him over to me, and You will see that Your servant will murmur against You and curse Your name.” So God gave up the just man He loved so much into the devil’s hands. And the devil struck down his children and his cattle and scattered his wealth, all at once, like a thunderbolt from heaven. Job tore his mantle and fell to the ground and cried aloud, “Naked came I out of my mother’s womb, and naked shall I return into the earth. The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever and ever.”

Fathers and teachers, forgive my tears, for all my childhood rises up before me again. I breathe as I breathed then, with the breast of a little child of eight, and I feel what I felt then: awe and wonder and gladness. The camels caught my imagination. So did Satan, who spoke with God like that, and God, who gave His servant up to ruin, and His servant crying out, “Blessed be Your name although You punish me.” Then there was the soft, sweet singing in the church, “Let my prayer rise up before You,” and again the incense from the priest’s censer, and the kneeling and the prayer. Ever since then (only yesterday I read it once more) I have not been able to read that sacred tale without tears. How much there is in it that is great, mysterious and unfathomable! Later I heard words of mockery and blame, proud words. “How could God hand over the most loved of His saints to amuse the devil? How could He take away his children, strike him with sore boils so that he scraped the matter from his sores with a piece of broken pot, and all for nothing, only to boast to the devil? ‘See what My saint can suffer for My sake.’” But the greatness of it lies just in its being a mystery. In it the passing show of this earth and the eternal truth are brought together. In the face of the earthly truth, the eternal truth is accomplished. On the first days of creation the Creator ended each day with praise: “It is good, what I have made.” So now He looks at Job and praises His creation again. And Job, in praising the Lord, serves not only Him but all His creation, for generations and generations and for ever and ever, since he was ordained for that. Good heavens, what a book it is, and what lessons are in it! What a book the Bible is, what a miracle, and what strength it gives to man! It is like a mold cast of the world, of man and of human nature. Everything is there, and a law for everything, for all the ages. And what mysteries are solved and revealed in it! God raises Job up again and gives him wealth again. Many years pass, and Job has other children and loves them. But how could he love those new ones, when the first children are gone, when he has lost them? Remembering them, how could he be fully happy with the new ones, however dear they might be? But he could, he could. This is the great mystery of human life: old grief passes gradually into quiet, tender joy. The mild serenity of old age takes the place of the riotous blood of youth. Each day I bless the rising sun, and my heart still sings to meet it, as before. But now I love its setting even more, with its long slanting rays, and the soft, tender, gentle memories that come with them, the dear images from my whole long, happy life. And over all of it the Divine Truth, softening, reconciling, forgiving! My life is ending, I know that well. But every day that is left to me, I feel how my earthly life touches a new life, infinite and unknown, a life that is drawing near. Its nearness sets my soul quivering with rapture, my mind glowing and my heart weeping with joy.

Friends and teachers, I have heard more than once, and lately one hears it more often, that priests, and above all village priests, complain on every side of their miserable income and their humiliating lot. They state plainly, even in print (I have read it myself), that because of their small means they are unable to teach the Scriptures to the people. And if Lutherans and heretics come and lead the flock astray, they say, they let them do it, because they have so little to live on. May the Lord increase the sustenance that is so precious to them, for their complaint is just. But truly I tell you, if anyone is to blame in this matter, half the fault is ours. The priest may be short of time. He may say truly that he is crushed all the while with work and services. Yet it is not all his time. Even he has one hour a week to remember God. And he does not work the whole year round. Let him gather people around him once a week, for an hour in the evening, if only the children at first. The fathers will hear of it, and they too will begin to come. There is no need to build halls for this. Let him take them into his own cottage. They will not spoil his cottage, because they will only be there for an hour. Let him open that book and begin to read it. Let him do it without grand words or superciliousness, without condescension, but gently and kindly, glad that he is reading to them and that they are listening attentively, loving the words himself, and stopping only now and then to explain a word the peasants do not understand. Do not be anxious. They will understand everything. The Orthodox heart will understand all! Let him read them about Abraham and Sarah, about Isaac and Rebecca, about how Jacob went to Laban and wrestled with the Lord in his dream and said, “This place is holy.” He will make an impression on the devout mind of the peasant. Let him read, especially to the children, how the brothers sold Joseph into bondage, the tender boy, the dreamer and prophet. Let him read how they told their father that a wild beast had devoured him, and showed him his blood-stained clothes. Let him read how the brothers afterwards journeyed into Egypt for corn. Joseph, by then a great ruler, was not recognized by them, and he tormented them, accused them and kept back his brother Benjamin, and all through love: “I love you, and loving you I torment you.” For all his life he remembered how they had sold him to the merchants in the burning desert, by the well, and how he had wrung his hands and wept and begged his brothers not to sell him as a slave in a strange land. And now, seeing them again after many years, he loved them beyond measure, but out of love he harassed and tormented them. In the end he left them, unable to bear the suffering of his heart, flung himself on his bed and wept. Then he wiped away his tears and went out to them joyful, and told them, “Brothers, I am your brother Joseph!” Let him read them further how happy old Jacob was to learn that his darling boy was still alive. Let him read how Jacob left his own country and went to Egypt, and died in a foreign land. He left behind his great prophecy, which had lain mysteriously hidden all his life in his meek and timid heart: that from his offspring, from Judah, would come the great hope of the world, the Messiah and Saviour.

Fathers and teachers, forgive me, and do not be angry that I have been babbling like a little child about what you have long known, and can teach me a hundred times more skillfully. I speak only out of rapture, and forgive my tears, for I love the Bible. Let him weep too, the priest of God, and let him be sure that the hearts of his listeners will throb in answer. Only a tiny little seed is needed. Drop it into the heart of the peasant and it will not die. It will live in his soul all his life, hidden amid his darkness and sin like a bright spot, like a great reminder. And there is no need of much teaching or explaining. He will understand it all simply. Do you suppose the peasants do not understand? Try reading them the touching story of the fair Esther and the haughty Vashti, or the miraculous story of Jonah in the whale. Do not forget the parables of Our Lord either. Choose especially from the Gospel of St. Luke (that is what I did). Then take from the Acts of the Apostles the conversion of St. Paul, which you must not leave out on any account. And from the _Lives of the Saints_ take, for instance, the life of Alexey, the man of God, and the greatest of all, the happy martyr and seer of God, Mary of Egypt. With these simple tales you will pierce their hearts. Give one hour a week to it in spite of your poverty, only one little hour. And you will see for yourselves that our people are gracious and grateful, and will repay you a hundredfold. They will remember the kindness of their priest and the moving words they heard from him. Of their own accord they will help him in his fields and in his house, and will treat him with more respect than before, so that his worldly well-being will even increase. The thing is so simple that sometimes one is afraid to say it, for fear of being laughed at. And yet how true it is! One who does not believe in God will not believe in God’s people. One who believes in God’s people will see His Holiness too, even if he had not believed in it until then. Only the people, and their spiritual power in the future, will convert our atheists, who have torn themselves away from their native soil.
And what use are Christ’s words unless we set an example? The people are lost without the Word of God, for their souls thirst for the Word and for all that is good.

In my youth, long ago, nearly forty years ago, I traveled all over Russia with Father Anfim, collecting funds for our monastery. One night we stayed with some fishermen on the bank of a great navigable river. A good-looking peasant lad of about eighteen joined us. He had to hurry back the next morning to tow a merchant’s barge along the bank. I noticed that he looked straight ahead with clear and tender eyes. It was a bright, warm, still night in July. A cool mist rose from the broad river. We could hear a fish splash, the birds were quiet, and everything was hushed and beautiful, everything praying to God. Only we two were awake, the lad and I, and we talked about the beauty of this world of God’s and the great mystery of it. Every blade of grass, every insect, ant and golden bee, knows its path so marvelously, though it has no intelligence. They bear witness to the mystery of God and keep accomplishing it themselves. I saw that the dear lad’s heart was moved. He told me that he loved the forest and the forest birds. He was a bird-catcher. He knew the call of each bird and could summon any of them. “I know nothing better than being in the forest,” said he, “though all things are good.”

“Truly,” I answered him, “all things are good and fair, because all is truth. Look,” said I, “at the horse, that great beast so close to man. Or look at the lowly, thoughtful ox, which feeds him and works for him. Look at their faces: what meekness, what devotion to man, who often beats them without mercy. What gentleness, what trust and what beauty! It is touching to know that there is no sin in them, for all, all except man, is sinless, and Christ was with them before us.”
“Why,” asked the boy, “is Christ with them too?”

“It cannot but be so,” said I, “since the Word is for all. All creation and all creatures, every leaf, strive toward the Word. They sing glory to God and weep to Christ, accomplishing this without knowing it, through the mystery of their sinless life. Over there,” said I, “in the forest, the dreadful bear roams, fierce and menacing, and yet innocent in it.” And I told him how a bear once came to a great saint who had taken refuge in a tiny cell in the wood. The saint pitied him. He went up to him without fear and gave him a piece of bread. “Go along,” said he, “Christ be with you,” and the savage beast went away meekly and obediently, doing no harm. The lad was delighted that the bear had gone away without hurting the saint, and that Christ was with him too. “Ah,” said he, “how good that is, how good and beautiful is all God’s work!” He sat musing, quietly and sweetly. I saw that he understood. And he slept beside me, a light and sinless sleep. May God bless youth! And I prayed for him as I went to sleep. Lord, send peace and light to Your people!
